evidence.text: And, and so I think, wrapping up my thought, like since, you know, for me, I understand this is early days, but I’m very much a person of like go-to-market first, do everything you can to de-risk go to market first, and so I’m going to be a pass. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: All right. My name is Tiffany. I’m one of the three founders of Metapyxl, along with my husband John and my sister Jennifer.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Family business.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Nice.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: John and I have actually been working together for 20 years as commercial photographers. Everything we shoot goes online. And uh what we realized is the internet really is the world’s largest copy machine. And the work is then subject to theft and misappropriation, leading to loss of revenue and authorship. In fact, 2.5 billion images are stolen daily on a global level. And I am literally freezing up here.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: So what do you do and how do you do it?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: No, no, I’m getting there, I’m getting there. Do you mind? I’m sorry.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: No, no. Take your time.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Okay. Um. They’re being stolen on a global level. And I have fear of public speaking.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Oh, it’s okay.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: It's okay.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: We can make it more conversational.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Yeah, we can have a conversation.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Why don’t we just chat.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: It doesn’t have to be like a speech.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: No, no, no it’s fine, I’ve got this. I’ve got this.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: All right.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Thank you. Um. Um, oh, okay. I'm ready.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Excellent.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: In fact, 2.5 billion images are stolen daily on a global level and of course this is what we experience firsthand. That's how Metapyxl was born. And it was born out of a need to track, protect and promote digital media. And we do so by applying a proactive, survivable meta mark, as we're calling it, into media. And you can think of the meta mark as like an invisible fingerprint protecting it with permanent metadata. And it survives everything from screenshots, cropping and compression.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Wow.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: We then take our Metapyxl platform on to the blockchain and we leverage it with a smart contract. And we are here today currently seeking $850,000 to help finalize our MVP and pay for our legal and IP costs.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: I also have a little demo here.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Yeah, let's see it.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Oh yeah, sure.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: We’d love to see it.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: You click on the image, it has all the creator’s information. And it shows you who the licensor is. It’s registered on the blockchain. That way you always know where it is, who’s owning it. And uh, it keeps track of your attribution.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: And um what if I just take a screenshot of it. So how, how would that work? If I, what if I just took a screenshot of that and put it on my website?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Yeah. So that’s the beautiful thing about our core technology, is that it actually embeds into any media. And so it becomes part of the work.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Could you just keep going on that. How does it actually do that?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: So um, if you were to sprinkle glitter let’s say on an image, it’s in every single part of that image.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So you're saying of we took a screenshot of that, we would see a picture that has, like...

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: No. So if you took a screenshot of this and then try...

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: ...glitter.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: No. No. It's invisible.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: So if you took a screenshot and then you tried to pass it off as your own and put it back online, because it already has that mark in there, that unique fingerprint, it would recognize whose image it is. It helps to track that image, always know where it is online, know who the creator is Always…

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: That's not answering my question. So, if I, if I take a screenshot of that image and put it on my blog, how will you get notified that I've done that?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Yeah. So. Um, through the technology. It is always attributed to that image.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Let me see if this is the question. So we get that your technology tracks it. Is there a proactive notification?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Yes.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Or would someone have to say, Where is this image being used?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: No, it, it lets you know. It tells you. There's proactive notification at all times.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: But I don't understand how that's possible.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: You want to know how does it phone home?

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: It’s through an invisible fingerprint, basically.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Where are you in terms of your development?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Okay. So we are currently developing the MVP.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: And when you say that, you mean like there, there isn’t any form of a product built today?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Correct. Yes. Other than the fact that it’s been proven, the technology is ready to go. We’ve spoken to everyone to be able to build this out. And ultimately, once we get our funding, it’ll be about four months until it’s finished.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How do you make money in this model?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Well, we are looking at it as a SaaS and licensing structure.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So if I were a photographer, I would pay some monthly subscription to use this?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Correct. Just like anybody that's now using Dropbox or that sort of thing. It comes part of your daily routine.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: So what would they pay?

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: How much are they gonna pay? Yeah.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Well, we haven't set up that yet because we're still trying to figure out how much it's going to cost to ultimately finalize this product.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So right now, are you guys actively selling ah this product?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Not currently. Right now we’re just developing it. But we’re getting everybody, you know, we’re obviously trying to get people on board so that it, when it’s ready, we’ll have the beta customers, which, the EU, they have an urgent need for this type, type of technology. Their digital single market legislation was just passed.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: It’s going to be put towards the platforms to take responsibility for maintaining the rights of the content creators.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Oh, so, is, is that what it is? Cos like, when I first heard this, and I was actually pretty intrigued, it seemed like it was every brand, company, photographer, who just can like sign up for their $20 a month and get like their Life Lock for their own images.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Yep.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Exactly.

turns.speaker: David
turns.text: Well. But then it sounds like. Well but then you start talking about governments and legislation that I've never heard of.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Sorry. It’s a big, it’s a big offer. Right. Of course. But you know, we’ve spoken to a ton of different photographers who would be completely on board. We’ve spoken to celebrities and I’m not going to name who but, ah, We’ve already got, also on our advisory panel, another photographer, Jill Greenberg, and she is going to be a beta customer as well.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: I think it's cool that so many people could be interested in this, right, and like that's what makes it a big problem and a big business. Um, but I, I worry it's gonna be impossibly hard for you guys to kind of get out of the gate without like a really crisp initial customer. And like exactly who that target demo is, what their problem is, how they solve it today, and why your solution is better, I think that's gotta be really locked down.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: I agree. And thankfully, you know, I'm not the only one in this company trying to figure that out.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: If I were in your position, I would just run with individual photographers...

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Of course.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: ...as the initial customer.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.speaker: Maia
turns.text: Because you know them. You speak their language, probably part of the community, you could get a lot of feedback from them to iterate on the product.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Absolutely 100%. But I, but we do see that locking this in for the enterprise platforms, it's a huge problem right now.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: I think everybody here invests in really early stage companies...

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Yep.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: … or we wouldn’t be on this panel. And I am just struggling to figure out, if you only could serve one customer for the next 18 to 24 months, who would you pick? Because I really am struggling to figure out, like, my concern hearing your presentation is you’re going to get 5% of the way with enterprise, 10% of the way with photographers, and you’re going to end up burning through $850k and you’re gonna know a little bit about a lot of customers, instead of a lot about a small number of customers. And to me, that’s like the recipe for startup death.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: And so like if you could only pick one customer segment, like who would you pick? To the exclusion of everyone else with full knowledge that there are other big opportunities out there.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Sure. Um, I would pick myself.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Photographers.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Yeah. Of course. And I didn’t mean to suggest that we weren’t understanding that. I’m just, you know, obviously kind of caught between knowing that these platforms are imminently looking to solve this problem. But also knowing that people like me are gonna really find value in this. So yeah, we would start with people like me.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So, I’m gonna be really direct with you. I’ve actually seen a lot of businesses try and go after this same opportunity and I fully believe that there’s a big, big problem here. I think, from observing these other companies that do have developed products, I think, at the end of the day, the biggest struggle actually has been on the customer acquisition side. Getting people to pay for this. That’s what I would actually test first. You have a community of photographers who are in your network, can you pre-sell some of this?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: And I think from there you can then later sell to enterprises, if that looks promising.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Yeah, of course. I mean, I mean, we're not being silly thinking that we're gonna just go right out of the gate here and it's going to be perfect.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: And, and so I think, wrapping up my thought, like since, you know, for me, I understand this is early days, but I’m very much a person of like go-to-market first, do everything you can to de-risk go to market first, and so I’m going to be a pass. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Can you talk about your team.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Yeah. Our two developers, Chet and Mike, they work in cyber forensics and cyber technology. Our other team members, we have a CEO at the moment, um, working with us to, um, get this product done.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Who's the CEO?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Um. Bob Michaelson. He's, ah, brought four companies to exit. And M&A. He worked with Sterling Partners. Um. $5 billion. So we just signed him on recently.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: So I’m gonna ask you a really blunt question.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: If you have two developers and you have a CEO who is managing product, what is that the three of you as co-founders are working on?

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: My sister's out in San Francisco, and she handles the sales and marketing side of the company. Um, John and I are wearing many hats. John's a designer, and an artist, so he's helping with all of the branding and the look. And I was a producer, in a past life, so I help kind of bring everything together, on a daily basis.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: At the stage that we all invest, pre-seed, seed, the thing that I value most is the team. And your team structure is not set up for success, in my opinion.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: How so? Can I ask?

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Yeah, sure, of course. So this is actually pretty heavy technical lift.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Yep.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: So you’re doing like, um, photograph fingerprinting, there’s a blockchain component. And your team, like, you have three founders who are non-technical. In this business, I think technology is core to the product. So I want somebody with a technical background to be part of the founding team.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Well, okay. And just to put this out there our developer once we get some funding, he’s going to come on as our full-time CTO. Um. I don’t know if that changes your perspective here a little bit, but...

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: It doesn’t. Because you have, you have four other people that are more senior than this person. This person hasn’t committed. You know, it’s like…

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: How so? He hasn’t committed?

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: Like he’s committed to a job once you have money to invest. Or to give him. But um. It’s like, if technology was core to the business, he would be one of the top four people in the company.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Well, I, we consider him to be one of the top four people in the company.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: But you have three founders, a CEO, external CEO.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Correct.

turns.speaker: Sheel
turns.text: So, the other thing I’d say is, external CEO also is a red flag for me. At this stage in the company, a pre-seed company, a founder should probably be CEO. And so for that reason, I’m gonna pass.

turns.speaker: Tiffany
turns.text: Okay. Thank you.

turns.speaker: Charles
turns.text: So I’m gonna pass. I'm just really concerned about your team composition, honestly. Typically when we invest in companies at this stage, it’s 2 or 3 people and the question is always, What more can this team do with more resources? You have a rather large team for a company of your stage. And I think, my fear is like you have a team of 5 or 6? That’s already a little amorphous. And like adding more money might actually make the problem worse not better. So, my, I know it’s really hard, it’s a really harsh thing to say, I know. But I really, I would encourage you to like ask yourselves the really hard question, like, do all three of us need to be involved fulltime as cofounders in the business? Because I think it undermines your story right now. And I feel like there’s some good nuggets here, but I can’t get past that. And so for me, this is a pass.
